title: Meet the stave
goal: Read the five lines and four spaces
teach: Music is written on five lines called a stave. A clef tells you which pitches those lines represent. In treble clef, the lines from bottom to top are E G B D F. The spaces are F A C E.
steps: Count the five lines from the bottom upwards.
Use E G B D F for line notes.
The four spaces spell F A C E.
example: A note on the bottom line of the treble stave is E.
question: Which notes spell the treble-clef spaces from bottom to top?
hint: The spaces spell an English word.
why: The spaces are F, A, C and E.

title: How long is a note?
teach: A semibreve is worth four crotchet beats, a minim two, a crotchet one and a quaver half. A dot adds half the note's original value.
steps: Start with a crotchet: 1 beat.
A minim is 2 beats; a quaver is half a beat.
A dotted crotchet is 1 + ½ = 1½ beats.
example: A dotted minim lasts 2 + 1 = 3 crotchet beats.
question: How many quavers fit in one dotted crotchet?
hint: One crotchet is two quavers. The dot adds one more.
why: Two quavers plus one quaver make three.

title: Find the pulse
teach: The top number of a time signature helps show how notes are grouped. In 3/4 there are three crotchet beats. In 6/8 there are usually two dotted-crotchet beats, each split into three quavers.
steps: Clap three steady crotchet beats for 3/4.
Clap TWO larger beats for 6/8.
Say ONE-two-three TWO-two-three.
example: 6/8 is compound duple: two beats, each divided into three.
question: Which is compound duple time?
hint: Look for six quavers grouped in two sets of three.

title: Build a major scale
teach: A semitone is the smallest step on a piano keyboard. Two semitones make a tone. Major scales follow T T S T T T S.
steps: Begin on C.
Follow C D E F G A B C.
Notice the semitones E–F and B–C.
example: G major needs F♯ to preserve the major-scale pattern.
question: What is the major-scale step pattern?
choices: T S T T S T T
T T S T T T S
T T T S T S T
hint: There is a semitone between degrees 3–4 and 7–8.
why: Major scales use tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone.

title: Unlock key signatures
teach: Key signatures show which notes are usually sharp or flat. Sharps are added in this order: F C G D A E B. Each new sharp key moves a perfect fifth higher.
steps: G major has F♯.
D major has F♯ and C♯.
A major adds G♯; E major adds D♯; B major adds A♯.
example: B major has five sharps: F♯ C♯ G♯ D♯ A♯.
question: How many sharps are in B major?
hint: Count G, D, A, E, B major along the circle of fifths.

title: Major and minor relatives
teach: Every major key has a relative minor sharing its key signature. The relative minor begins on the sixth note of the major scale, or three semitones below the major tonic.
steps: Write E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C D.
The sixth note is C.
Therefore E♭ major and C minor have the same three flats.
example: C major and A minor share no sharps or flats.
question: What is the relative minor of E♭ major?
hint: Count to the sixth note of E♭ major.
why: C minor shares E♭ major's three-flat signature.

title: Measure the distance
teach: An interval is the distance between two notes. Count letter names inclusively to get its number. Then check the semitones to determine major, minor, perfect, augmented or diminished.
steps: C to E spans C-D-E: a third.
C to E is four semitones: a major third.
Lower E to E♭: three semitones, a minor third.
example: C to G is a perfect fifth.
question: What interval is C up to E♭?
hint: It spans three letters, but E♭ is a semitone lower than E.

title: Move a melody
teach: Transposing moves every note by the same musical interval. Preserve the letter-name distance and the correct accidental; do not merely count white piano keys.
steps: Move C up a major second to D.
Move E up a major second to F♯.
Check the new key signature and any accidentals.
example: C–E transposed up a major second becomes D–F♯.
question: What is E transposed up a major second?
hint: A major second is two semitones.
why: E to F♯ is two semitones and spans two letter names.

title: Build a triad
teach: A triad is made from three notes stacked in thirds. In a major key, the tonic triad uses scale degrees 1, 3 and 5. Its root names the chord.
steps: Write C major: C D E F G A B.
Choose scale notes 1, 3 and 5.
You get C–E–G, the tonic triad.
example: The tonic triad of G major is G–B–D.
question: Which is the tonic triad in G major?
hint: Choose the first, third and fifth notes of G major.

title: Hear a musical ending
teach: A cadence is a pair of chords that creates a musical punctuation mark. Perfect cadences move V–I and sound final. Plagal cadences move IV–I. Imperfect cadences end on V.
steps: In C major, chord V is G major.
Chord I is C major.
V–I is a perfect cadence.
example: G major followed by C major is a perfect cadence in C major.
question: Which chord movement is a perfect cadence?
hint: The dominant resolves to the tonic.

title: Read the composer's instructions
teach: Composers use terms to describe tempo, mood and expression. Con moto means 'with movement'; dolce means 'sweetly'; ritardando means gradually slowing down.
steps: Read the word aloud.
Link it to an English relative: moto → motion.
Imagine how you would play the music.
example: Allegro con moto suggests lively music with movement.
question: What does con moto mean?

title: Meet the orchestra
teach: Orchestral instruments are grouped into strings, woodwind, brass and percussion. Bassoon, oboe, clarinet and flute are woodwind instruments; the flute is usually played without a reed.
steps: Listen for how sound begins.
Bassoon uses a double reed.
Trumpet uses buzzing lips in a brass mouthpiece.
example: Bassoon and oboe both use double reeds.
question: Which instrument uses a double reed?
hint: It is a low-pitched woodwind instrument.
why: The bassoon uses a double reed.
